paper.title: Digital skill adoption and employment dynamics: Evidence from matched vacancy-employer–employee data
paper.code_data_availability: Data availability: 'The data that has been used is confidential.' (p. 22). The work was supported by the ROCKWOOL Foundation, Denmark (project 3034); no DST project number is given.

registers.name_in_paper: Job postings data from HBS Economics
variables_mentioned: full text of each job posting

registers.name_in_paper: VITU (survey data on firms' IT expenditures)

linkages: job postings matched to firm-year observations in the firm register via unique firm identifiers; where the posting text carries no identifier, HBS Economics imputes it from the firm name, and matches with more than five letters' difference are dropped
firms linked to their individual employees via firm identifiers in the register data
employee demographics (country of birth, gender) merged from the BEF-register to the employee data
VITU IT-expenditure survey responses matched to firm-year observations by firm identifier (25% of firm-year observations)

sample.universe: Danish private-sector firms outside the IT industries, 2008-2019
selection_rules: merge annual job postings data to the firm register by firm identifier
drop job postings from firms with more job posts than employees in a given year (recruitment agencies)
drop firms operating primarily in the IT industries (JUR_HOVED_BRA_DB07 starting with 62, 631 or 582)
drop firms with an average number of full-time equivalent employees below 20 from 2008 to 2019
exclude firms that never posted any job vacancy in the period
for Table 3, retain observations with non-missing data for all firm-based variables
sample.n_observations: 75,799 firm-year observations (7779 firms) in Tables 2, 4 and 5; 74,915 firm-year observations (7762 firms) in Table 3; 20,410-22,846 firm-year observations (5349-5946 firms) in the lead-lag figures; approximately 450,000 job posts from over 7500 distinct firms

construction_notes: digital skills are extracted from vacancy text in three steps: a fine-tuned BERT NER model extracts skill tokens, a second BERT model classifies tokens as digital or non-digital, and a third assigns digital tokens to one of eight digital skill clusters following Nania et al. (2019); Danish-language posts use the Maltehb/danish-bert-botxo model
a job post is categorized into a digital skill cluster if it includes at least one token classified as such, and may fall into several clusters
the firm-level measure is the annual share of the firm's job posts including the skill requirement
the digitalization measure D_it enters the estimating equations in levels, not logs, because the shares are fractional with many zeros
monthly employee records are converted to yearly full-time equivalents within each category (e.g. by gender)
all monetary values are inflation-adjusted to 2015-levels using the yearly CPI
where exports are zero, the log is replaced by zero and a binary indicator for the original zero is included (Table 3)

TFP is estimated from the log production function by one-digit industry with the Wooldridge (2009) one-step GMM formulation of Levinsohn and Petrin (2003), using log intermediate inputs as proxy and third-order polynomials in the first stage
labor churning is defined as the difference between worker flows and job reallocation (Burgess et al., 2000)
occupations follow the International Classification of Occupations (ISCO), 1-digit
in Appendix B a digitalization event is the first year in which vacancies including any digital skill exceed 7.5% of the firm's full-time-equivalent employment (3.25% for data science & AI skills)

claims.statement: Larger firms post a higher share of vacancies demanding digital skills.

treatment.label: ln(employment)

register_source.value: BFL-register (monthly employee records on earnings, hours worked and occupation), aggregated to yearly full-time equivalents

definition.value: natural logarithm of the firm's number of full-time-equivalent employees in the year

timing.value: measured in the same firm-year as the outcome

register_source.value: Job postings data from HBS Economics covering virtually all Danish online job postings 2008–2019 (full vacancy text), matched to firms by firm identifier; not a Danish administrative register

definition.value: the share of vacancies demanding digital skills (column 1 of Table 3)

timing.value: annual share, measured in the same firm-year as the regressors

units.value: share of vacancies demanding the given skill type (0-1) per one-unit increase in the regressor

estimand.target_population: Danish private-sector firms outside the IT industries with an average of at least 20 full-time-equivalent employees over 2008–2019 that post vacancies
estimand.time_horizon: contemporaneous: regressor and outcome measured in the same firm-year

population.description: Danish private-sector firm-year observations, 2008–2019, from firms with an average of at least 20 full-time-equivalent employees over 2008–2019 that posted at least one vacancy in the period, excluding firms operating primarily in IT industries
population.selection: firms with mean full-time-equivalent employment below 20 over 2008–2019 dropped; firms that never posted a job vacancy in the period dropped; firms operating primarily in IT industries dropped; job postings from firms with more job posts than employees in a given year dropped

identification.source_of_variation: cross-firm and within-firm variation over 2008–2019 in the share of a firm's vacancies that demand digital skills; no exogenous shock is used

key_assumptions.assumption: Digital skill demand expressed in job postings reflects the adoption of digital technologies within the firm
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 2 (IT expenditure percentile rank against the share of digital job posts) and Table A.1

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimated associations are not interpreted as causal effects

threats_discussed: digitalization is observed only for firms that post vacancies demanding digital skills; firms that retrain workers in-house or hired digital capacity before 2008 are missed
robustness_checks: controlling for the share of vacancies demanding cognitive and social skills
validation of the digital-skill measure against VITU survey IT expenditure (Fig. 2, Table A.1)

estimation.specification: OLS of the annual firm-level share of digital job posts on firm characteristics; no fixed effects reported
controls: Share emp., foreign

ambiguities: Table 3 is a descriptive regression of the digital-skill share on firm characteristics; the paper asserts no direction of causation, so no causal edge is recorded.

evidence.how: Table 3 reports standard errors in parentheses; no confidence interval is printed.
The paper states the average share of digital vacancies in the sample is 32%; expressed in the outcome's own units (a 0-1 share) that is 0.32.

identification.source_of_variation: the first year in which a firm posts vacancies including any digital skill exceeding 7.5% of its full-time-equivalent employment (3.25% for data science & AI skills), for events in 2012–2014, with firms experiencing similar events five or more years later as controls

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: firms experiencing a digitalization event in 2012–2014 and firms experiencing a similar event five or more years later would have followed the same employment path absent the event
key_assumptions.supported_by: pre-event coefficients in Figs. B.1–B.6; k = -1 is the omitted base period

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation of the digitalization event in the four pre-event years
key_assumptions.supported_by: pre-event coefficients plotted for k = -4,...,-2

key_assumptions.assumption: The treated sample is conditioned on having a clear digitalization event in 2012–2014, and the control sample on having one five or more years later
key_assumptions.supported_by: the authors note the method significantly reduces the sample size of treated firms

implies_edges.from: timing of the firm's first large digital-skill vacancy spike

key_assumptions.assumption: Digital skill demand expressed in job postings reflects the adoption of digital technologies within the firm
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 2 and Table A.1

threats_discussed: significantly reduced sample size of treated firms
heterogeneous treatment effects across cohorts in the main two-way fixed-effects specification, which this design relaxes
robustness_checks: alternative control group of firms experiencing similar digitalization events exactly five years later
unresolved_confounders: unobserved time-varying firm-level factors that simultaneously drive digital hiring intensity and employment growth

estimation.specification: stacked difference-in-differences event study, Eq. (6), treated firms with a digitalization event in 2012-2014 against firms with a similar event five or more years later; k = -1 omitted
fixed_effects: year-by-the share of employees with an IT degree in 2008
controls: indicator for no job postings in the year
trend in the firm's 2008 share of employees with an IT degree

heterogeneity.finding: similar variation in effects at the regional level as in Fig. 10, the only exception being no temporary effect in Central Jutland

evidence.annotation: The dependent variables are the log of firm-level employment. All regressions are estimated by OLS separately for each region.

evidence.how: Figure B.6 plots point estimates with 95% confidence intervals but prints no numeric coefficient, standard error, interval endpoint or p-value.
No mean or standard deviation of the outcome is printed for this figure.

value.as_printed: E_ity = sum_{k=-4, k!=-1}^{4} (delta_k . 1[k = t] . D_i + theta_k . 1[k = t]) + mu_i + eta_iy + lambda_sry + rho_iy + epsilon_ity
value.lhs: E_ity, firm-level employment and other outcomes for firm i in year y relative to the event
value.normalisation: k = -1, the year before the digitalization event, is the omitted base period

falsification.condition: a systematic relationship between a firm's digital investments and its employment levels in future years, before the investment occurred, would indicate anticipation and violate the model's assumptions
